1  ORAL JUDGMENT 1.

In this appeal, filed under Section 23 of the Railway 2 FA26.12 (J) final.odt Claims Tribunal Act,
1987 (hereinafter referred to as "the Act of 1987"
for short), the challenge is to the judgment and order dated July 5, 2011, passed by the Railway Claims Tribunal, Nagpur Bench, Nagpur, whereby the claim for compensation filed by the appellants came to be dismissed.

entities.text: Railway Claims Tribunal, Nagpur Bench, Nagpur
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text:
2. Background facts:
Appellant No. 1 is the wife of the deceased, and appellant Nos. 2 to 4 are the children of the deceased.

The appellants claim that on April 30, 2010, deceased Vinayak @
Vinod Ganuji Deshmukh with his friend Gopal Narayan Gedam went to Shegaon to offer prayer at Ganajan Maharaj Temple.
After offering prayers, they purchased a joint journey ticket to come back to Chandrapur.
It is stated that on the way, after Dhamangaon Railway Station, the deceased fell from a running train due a sudden jerk to the train.
They claim that there was an overcrowding of passengers on the train.
The deceased succumbed to the injuries sustained in the accident.
According to them, the death was in an untoward incident.
They claim that they are entitled to get compensation.
3 FA26.12 (J) final.odt 3.
The respondent--Railway filed a written statement and opposed the claim.
It is the case of the respondent that the death was due to the negligent act of the deceased.
The deceased was either sitting at the door or footsteps of the coach and, therefore, fell from the moving train and died.
The death was not in an untoward incident.
The deceased was not a bona fide passenger travelling with a valid journey ticket.
4. The parties have adduced evidence before the Tribunal.
Learned Member of the Tribunal, on consideration of the evidence on record, held that the deceased was not a bona fide passenger as well as death was not in an untoward incident.
Being aggrieved by these findings, the appellants have come before this Court in appeal.

5. I have heard Mr. S. B. Dhande, learned advocate for the appellants and Ms. Neeraja Choube,
learned advocate for the respondent.
Perused the record and proceedings.

6. In the facts and circumstances, the following points fall under my determination :-
4 FA26.12 (J) final.odt i] Whether the deceased was a bona fide passenger travelling by the train in question with a valid journey ticket ?
Smt. Tarabai Wd/O Vinayak @ Vinod ... vs Union Of India Through General Manager, ... on 15 January, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/182169003/
2 ii] Whether the deceased died in an untoward incident within the meaning of Section 123(c) of the Railways Act, 1989 ?
7.

Learned advocate Mr. S. B. Dhande for the appellants submitted that there is ample evidence to prove that the deceased was a bona fide passenger travelling with a valid journey ticket from Shegaon to Chandrapur.
Learned advocate pointed out that the journey ticket, which was collected by the police during the course of inquiry, was part of the record.
The railway ticket corroborates the oral evidence of AW2 Gopal Gedam, who was a co-passenger with the deceased.

Learned advocate submitted that the defence of negligence or contributory negligence is not available to the respondent-Railway inasmuch as the liability is a strict liability, or the liability is based on 'no fault theory'.
Learned advocate submitted that there is ample evidence to prove that The deceased died due to the injuries sustained in the accident and as such that the death was in an untoward incident.
8. Learned advocate Ms. N.G. Choube for the respondent Railway, in short, supported the judgment and order passed by the 5 FA26.12 (J) final.odt Tribunal.
Learned advocate submitted that the evidence is completely silent as to who had handed over the journey ticket to the police during the course of the investigation.
Learned advocate further submitted that the DRM inquiry revealed that the deceased was standing at the door of the coach and, therefore, fell from the moving train.
Learned advocate submitted that learned Member of the Tribunal was right in holding that the deceased was solely responsible for this incident.
9. In order to appreciate the rival contentions, I have gone through the record and proceedings.
On going through the record and proceedings, I am constrained to observe at the outset that on both the counts, the findings of fact recorded by learned Member of the Tribunal cannot be sustained.
Learned Member of the Tribunal, in my view, has not appreciated the evidence on record in proper perspective.
AW1, the wife of the deceased, was not travelling with the deceased at the relevant time.
AW2 Gopal was travelling with the deceased.
In this case, undisputedly, the journey ticket from Shegaon to Chandrapur was recovered during the course of the investigation.
The journey ticket is on record, which is marked as Exh.AW1/1.
The said ticket was for the journey from Shegaon to Chandrapur for two adult passengers.
It was 6 FA26.12 (J) final.odt purchased at 15.18 hours.
The incident, undisputedly, occurred at 9.15 p.m.
The DRM's report is on record.
Similarly, the report made by the Inspector of RPF is part of the record.
In the RPF report, there is a reference to the journey ticket with its number.
It is undisputed that an investigation of the incident was conducted by Dattapur Police Station, Dhamangaon.
The ticket, which is produced on record in this case, was part of that record.

Evidence of AW1 that the deceased and co- passenger Gopal boarded the Bhusawal passenger train at Shegaon with valid journey ticket, has been fully corroborated by the journey ticket, which is available on record.
This evidence, in my view, is sufficient to discharge the initial burden cast on the appellants and prove that the deceased was a bona fide passenger travelling with a valid journey ticket.
It was necessary on the part of the respondent--Railway to adduce evidence to disprove this fact.
Learned Member of the Tribunal, as can be seen from the record, has not properly appreciated this material.
It is not the case of the respondent--Railway that the journey ticket was either manipulated or planted to create evidence.
In the teeth of the available evidence, such an inference is not possible as well.
Accordingly, I conclude that, at this point, the finding recorded by the learned Member of the Tribunal cannot be sustained.

The next important issue is with regard to the death of the deceased in an untoward incident.
AW1 Gopal, friend of the deceased, as a co-passenger, has narrated the first-hand account of the incident before the Tribunal.
He has stated that the train was overcrowded.
He has stated that the deceased had gone to attend nature's call, and due to sudden jerk, fell from a running train after Dhamangaon railway station.
He has stated that he did not pull the chain because of the objection of the co-passengers.
He has stated that after reaching the next station, i.e. Pulgaon railway station, he informed the Station Master of Pulgaon railway station about the incident.
The Station Master of Pulgaon railway station directed him to go to Dhamangaon railway station and report it to the Station Master of Dhamangaon railway station.
He went there and reported the incident to the Station Master of Dhamangaon railway station.
It has come on record that the Station Master of Dhamangaon railway station directed him to go to the police station and report the matter to the police.
Accordingly, he went to Dattapur police station, Dhamangaon and reported the matter to the police.
An investigation was conducted by the Dattapur police station, Dhamangaon.
8 FA26.12 (J) final.odt 11.
An inquiry was conducted by RPF.
The DRM also conducted an inquiry, and the report of the DRM is on record.
The DRM's report concludes that the deceased might have been standing at the door or at the footsteps of the coach, and due to his negligence, he might have fallen from a moving train.
In short, it is the case of the Railway that the incident occurred due to the negligence of the deceased.
The statement of AW2, a co-passenger, was recorded by the police.
It is true that there are some inconsistencies in his two statements.
The question is whether those inconsistencies by itself would be sufficient to discard his evidence ?
It is evident on perusal of the record that his evidence cannot be discarded on the basis of those inconsistencies.
Those inconsistencies, even if considered at its face value, would show that those are of no consequence.
12. The deceased was travelling with a valid journey ticket.
AW2 Gopal has stated that there was overcrowding on the train.
The deceased had gone to attend nature's call, and due to a sudden jerk to the train, he fell from the running train.
No evidence has been adduced by the respondent--Railway to rebut this evidence.
The respondent 9 FA26.12 (J) final.odt could have adduced evidence that there was no rush on the train.
The respondent should have established that there was no fall of any passenger from running train due to a sudden jerk or jolt to the train.

It appears on the basis of the record that the Station Master at Pulgaon as well as the Station Master at Dhamangaon Railway, did not bother to even listen to AW2 when he went to report the incident to them.
The first question is whether there is evidence as to the negligence of the deceased ?
The second question is whether defence of negligence or contributory negligence is available to the respondent-Railway ?
If a case falls under any of the clauses of the Proviso to Section 124-A of the Railway Act, 1989, then the claim for compensation is bound to fail.
If it is not so, then the case would squarely fall within the first part of Section 124A of the Act of 1989.
In that event, the Railway would be responsible to pay the compensation.

sentences.text: In my view, the case of the appellants is squarely covered by the decision of the Hon'ble Apex Court in Union of India .vs. Rina Devi, reported at AIR 2018 SC 2362.

entities.text: Union of India .vs. Rina Devi, reported at AIR 2018 SC 2362
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Paragraph 16.6 of the decision would be relevant for this purpose.

It is extracted below :-
"16.6

We are unable to uphold the above view as the concept of 'self-inflicted injury'
would require intention to 10 FA26.12 (J) final.odt inflict such injury and not mere negligence of any particular degree.
Doing so would amount to invoking the principle of contributory negligence which cannot be done in the case of liability based on 'no fault theory'.

We may in this connection refer to judgment of this Court in United India Insurance Co. Ltd. Versus Sunil Kumar (2017 (13) SCALE 652) laying down that plea of negligence of the victim cannot be allowed in claim based on 'no fault theory' under Section 163A of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988.

entities.text: United India Insurance Co. Ltd. Versus Sunil Kumar (2017 (13) SCALE 652)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
Accordingly, we hold that death or injury in the course of boarding or de- boarding a train will be an 'untoward incident' entitling a victim to the compensation and will not fall under the proviso to Section 124A merely on the plea of negligence of the victim as a contributing factor."
14. There is no evidence to show that the deceased was in any manner negligent.
In view of the law laid down as above, the defence of negligence or contributory negligence would not be available to the Railway.
The deceased was a bona fide passenger travelling with valid journey ticket.

Therefore,
the death in this case, was in an untoward incident.

15. The Hon'ble Apex Court in Union of India .vs. Prabhakaran Vijaya Kumar and others , reported at AIR 2009 SC (Supp) 383, has held that when two interpretations are possible, the interpretation that advances the object of the statute and serves its 11 FA26.12 (J) final.odt purpose should be preferred.

entities.text: Union of India .vs. Prabhakaran Vijaya Kumar and others , reported at AIR 2009 SC (Supp) 383
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It is held that this is required to be done because the provision for compensation in the Act is a beneficial piece of legislation.

It is further held that the expression 'accidental falling of a passenger from a train carrying passengers' in Section 123C of the Railways Act, 1989, includes accidents when a bona fide passenger is trying to enter the railway compartment and falls down during the process.
It is to be noted that the same principle would be applicable in case of a passenger, who has boarded the train with a valid journey ticket and falls from a moving train during the journey.
16. In the facts and circumstances, I conclude that the Tribunal was not right in rejecting the claim of the appellants.
The impugned judgment and order passed by the Tribunal cannot be sustained.
Accordingly, I record my findings on points nos. 1 and 2 in the affirmative.
The impugned judgment and order deserve to be set aside.
17. In this case, the accident occurred on April 30, 2010.

In view of the Notification issued by the Ministry of Railways (Railway Board) dated 22.12.2016, came into effect from 01.01.2017, in case of death claim, the claimant(s) is/are entitled to get compensation of Rs.

i] The judgment and order dated July 5, 2011, passed by the Railway Claims Tribunal, Nagpur Bench, Nagpur, is set aside.

iii] The amount be deposited directly in the bank accounts of the appellants.
The appellants are directed to provide their bank 13 FA26.12 (J) final.odt account details to the respondent--Railway.
iv] The appellants will not be entitled to any interest on the amount of compensation to be paid by the respondent.

v] Out of total compensation, appellant no. 1 shall be entitled to get 70% share, and appellant nos. 2,
